questions.title: What exactly is Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT) and how does it differ from additive low‑rank methods like LoRA?
questions.question_body:
I read that OFT updates a pretrained weight matrix $
\mathbf{W}^{0}$ by left‑multiplying an orthogonal matrix $
\mathbf{R}$ while LoRA adds a low‑rank product $
\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}^{\top}$. Could someone clarify why a multiplicative orthogonal transformation preserves pairwise neuron angles whereas an additive low‑rank update does not? Also, what practical consequences does this difference have on training stability and generalisation?

questions.title: How does Cayley parameterisation enforce orthogonality during training?
questions.question_body:
The paper uses $
\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ with $
\mathbf{Q}$ skew‑symmetric ($\mathbf{Q}=-\mathbf{Q}^{\top}$). I am unsure how this guarantees that $
\mathbf{R}$ stays orthogonal for any $
\mathbf{Q}$. Additionally, how is numerical stability handled when $(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})$ becomes close to singular during optimisation?

questions.title: Why does a block‑diagonal orthogonal matrix reduce trainable parameters, and what expressivity do we lose?
questions.question_body:
OFT introduces $
\mathbf{R}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{R}_1, \dots , \mathbf{R}_r)$ where each $
\mathbf{R}_i$ is $b \times b$ with $br=d$. I understand this reduces parameters from $O(d^2)$ to $O(bd)$, but I am confused about what kinds of transformations cannot be represented anymore when dimensions are split into independent blocks. Does this restriction affect the ability to capture cross‑block correlations?

questions.title: Can someone explain the construction of a butterfly factor $\bm B^{F}(k)$ in Equation (1)?
questions.question_body: Equation (1) defines $\bm B^{F}(k)= \begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf d_1)& \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf d_2)\\ \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf d_3)& \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf d_4) \end{bmatrix}$. What are the dimensions of each diagonal block $\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf d_i)$ relative to $k$? How do these four diagonal blocks combine to form a sparse matrix suitable for butterfly factorisation?

questions.title: How does butterfly factorisation achieve $O(d \log d)$ trainable parameters while representing a dense $d \times d$ orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that a product of $m=\log_2 d$ sparse matrices each having $O(d)$ non‑zero entries yields a dense orthogonal matrix with only $O(d \log d)$ parameters. Could someone walk through the parameter counting argument step by step, especially showing where the factor $(b-1)/2$ appears when using block size $b$?

questions.title: "Information transmission" view – how does it map matrix factorisation onto a grid graph?
questions.question_body: Section 3 describes representing $\mathbf R=\mathbf B_m \cdots \mathbf B_1$ as information flowing through a $d \times (m+1)$ node grid where each edge corresponds to a non‑zero entry of some $\mathbf B_i$. I would like a concrete illustration of how dense connectivity translates into constraints on edge placements across levels, and why each intermediate sparse matrix must contain at least $d$ edges.

questions.title: Why can a butterfly graph connect every source node to every sink node using only $O(d \log d)$ edges? A simple example would help.
questions.question_body: "The paper says that a butterfly topology achieves dense connectivity with just $8$ edges for $d=4$ (or similar)." Could anyone provide an explicit construction for, say, $d=8$, showing the sequence of sparse matrices and how information from node 1 eventually reaches node 7 after three stages?

questions.title: What exactly is “multiplicative dropout” for BOFT and why can’t standard dropout be used?
questions.question_body: "Standard dropout" zeroes out activations elementwise, but BOFT updates weights multiplicatively via an orthogonal matrix product. The authors propose dropping entire butterfly components ($p_1$%) and diagonal blocks within them ($p_2$%). How is this implemented in practice (e.g., masking which entries), and what intuition justifies these two separate dropout rates?

questions.title: Theorem 1 claims BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size – what does “expressive” mean here?
questions.question_body:
"Expressivity" seems related to covering more elements of the orthogonal group $
 O(d)$. The theorem states that concatenating products like $\bm B_{d-1,1}(d) \bm B^{\top}_{d-1,2}(d) \dots$ can approximate any orthogonal matrix. Could someone explain intuitively why alternating forward and transposed butterfly factors expands the reachable subspace compared to just one block‑diagonal OFT?

The paper gives $\text{	extbackslash{}#params}= \frac12(b-1)dm$ for BOFT$(m,b)$. I suspect this comes from counting independent entries in each skew‑symmetric generator $
 Q$, but I am not sure why there is a $(b-1)/2$ factor rather than simply $b(b-1)/2$. Could anyone derive this formula explicitly?

questions.title: Could you elaborate on the weight interpolation property illustrated in Figure 2?
questions.question_body:
Figure 2 shows that BOFT provides an intrinsic interpolation between the identity matrix and the learned orthogonal matrix. Since $
 R = \prod_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{

 R\, $? Is it simply scaling each skew‑symmetric generator or something else? Why is this property useful during finetuning?

 W^{0}||_{2}$ because $
 R$ is orthogonal. Could someone provide a short proof using singular value decomposition? Also, during training $
 R$ may deviate slightly from perfect orthogonality – does this affect spectral norm preservation?

questions.title: How can BOFT be interpreted as learning a bilinear similarity function?
questions.question_body:
The paper rewrites BOFT as learning $
 w^{0}_{i}\!^{\top}\! \n R \, x$, i.e., a bilinear form between pretrained neuron vector $
 w^{0}_{i}$ and input $
 x$. How does enforcing $
 R$ to be orthogonal relate to metric learning objectives such as learning Mahalanobis distances? Are there known benefits compared to unconstrained bilinear forms?

questions.title: What is required for identity initialization of all skew‑symmetric matrices in multiple butterfly components?
questions.question_body:
Each component uses Cayley transform with its own skew‑symmetric generator $
 Q_{j}$. To start from an overall identity transformation we need all products equal identity initially. Is it sufficient simply to set every $
 Q_{j}=0$, or do we also need special handling of permutations within each butterfly component?

questions.title: When applying BOFT to transformer models, should every linear projection be replaced by an orthogonal transformation?
questions.question_body: Transformers contain several linear layers per block (query/key/value projections, feed‑forward FC layers). The paper applies BOFT at "linear layers" – would you recommend applying it uniformly across all such layers or only at selected ones (e.g., attention projections)? Also, would placing OFT/BOFT before versus after layer normalisation change its effect?

questions.title: How should one choose $(m,b)$ per layer versus using a global configuration across layers?
questions.question_body: Different layers have different hidden dimensions ($d$). The paper presents BOFT$(m,b)$ where $m$ controls depth of factorisation and $b$ controls block size. In practice should we keep $(m,b)$ identical for all layers, or allocate larger budgets (larger $m$, smaller $b$) to deeper layers? What trade‑offs have been observed?

questions.title: Can classic transforms like DFT be exactly represented by an orthogonal butterfly matrix despite real‑valued constraints?
questions.question_body: Butterfly structures are known to implement FFT when complex numbers are allowed. Since BOFT restricts each sparse factor to be real orthogonal, can it still recover DFT exactly (perhaps up to scaling or permutations), or only approximate it? What modifications are needed if exact recovery is desired?

questions.title: How were random dense orthogonal matrices generated for the expressivity experiments (Anderson 1987)?
questions.question_body: Figure 4 approximates random dense orthogonal matrices of size 512×512 using BOFT variants. The citation refers to Anderson’s method – could anyone summarise how those matrices were sampled (e.g., via QR decomposition of Gaussian matrices), and whether alternative sampling methods would change the observed approximation error curves?
